prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clean case of a measurement technique that moved the limit of what can be measured. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light-shift problem while keeping thousands of atoms in a recoil- and Doppler-free regime, and the JILA work turned that into a clock with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 and coherence times that make many-body and spin-exchange effects visible. Concrete consequences already exist: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on fundamental-constant drift and on dark-matter couplings, relativistic geodesy, and the preparation of a redefinition of the second. Several independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) operate Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks and compare them, so reproducibility is not in doubt. All eight members place it in their top six and three rank it first, but I am arguing from the physics and not from the vote count. The attribution is as clean as these things get: a single decisive idea with an early demonstration, and a decisive realization to ultimate performance, with both names on the credited list.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and the risk of reading as a third metrology prize after Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency comb) and Wineland and Haroche (2012, control of single quantum systems, including the Al+ ion clock). A sceptic can say that the lattice clock is an incremental, if brilliant, evolution of precise spectroscopy and that the biggest payoffs (redefinition, geodesy, new-physics searches) are still prospective. Attribution beyond two names is also not fully settled: Lemonde and the Paris group, Lisdat and PTB, Ludlow and Oates at NIST, and Takamoto in the RIKEN work all contributed essential demonstrations, and I am working partly from memory on the order of the 1e-16 and 1e-18 milestones. I take these as real but not decisive. The comb prize recognised the ruler, the ion prize recognised control of single systems, and the lattice clock is a different principle, which uses many atoms in a trap that does not perturb the transition.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B018 (topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect) first, as a case where theory predicted a state and experiment realised it, and ranks B009 only sixth because of the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the appetite for another metrology prize.
responses.response: I accept that B018 has the prediction-plus-experiment structure that I also value, and the Molenkamp HgTe edge-channel measurement is a real experimental achievement. But I do not think it is the better prize on the evidence in the opening files. Your own attribution note says the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is outside the credited names and that the 3D work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Hasan) is a separate allocation problem, and Mehlig also flags the overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize. B009 has no comparable hole in its credit list. On the overlap argument, I would ask what the earlier prizes actually covered: the comb is a frequency ruler and the Wineland prize concerned control of single ions, while the lattice clock rests on a different principle, an ensemble in a magic-wavelength trap. Judged by that standard, B009 is at least as distinct from its predecessors as B018 is from 2016. I am not convinced yet that this removes your concern entirely, and I would like to hear what makes the 2005 and 2012 overlap decisive for you.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B008) first, argues that it is distinct from the 2025 prize, and himself notes a possible conflict as a director of a superconducting-circuits programme, and that Wallraff is missing from the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the point that circuit QED is real, well reproduced and enabling, and I ranked it fourth. My concern is the one you raise yourself: with Wallraff outside the credited list, the first strong-coupling experiment is not represented by the supplied configuration, and the 2025 prize is very recent and closely related in lineage. I would not want the committee to rank B008 first while that attribution gap and the timing question are open. Please also take seriously your own offer to defer on this candidate. I should also say plainly that WACQT puts you and me in a shared institutional network, so my ranking of B008 should not be taken as independent of that either, which is another reason I do not make it my preferred prize. On B009, we both rank it high, and I would value your view on whether the Ye group's coherence and spin-exchange results are best described in the citation or left to the background.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active matter (B005) first as a clean statistical-physics idea with three distinct decisive contributions, and ranks B009 sixth with a note on overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: The three-person map for active matter (Vicsek, Toner, Ramaswamy) is indeed clean, and I respect the generality of the idea. My difficulty is with the experimental side that you note yourself: the confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is partial and debated, and no other member ranks B005 at all. In the lab I would want a prediction to be quantitatively confirmed before it carries a prize citation, and for the lattice clock it is: intercomparisons between independent clocks agree at the 1e-18 level, which is about as strong a reproducibility test as physics offers. I would be glad to hear what the specific quantitative tests of the flocking transition are that persuade you that it is ready.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B009 first and B001 (atom interferometry) second, and notes that the credited trio for B001 is incomplete and that the discovery may be seen as an instrument family rather than a single discovery.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking of B009 and share your reasoning on reproducibility and timing. On B001 we are close, and I put it third. But I think your caveat deserves more weight than either of us gave it in the opening: Steven Chu, who with Kasevich demonstrated the light-pulse interferometer, is not on the credited list, the priority among Bordé, Pritchard, Mlynek and Kasevich is contested, and the field is more an instrument family than a single discovery. That is why I would keep B001 as an alternative and not as the preferred choice. If the committee wanted a second distinct part beside B009, B001 is the candidate I would look at most carefully, but with the three-person limit it would not fit with B009 without dropping a name from the pair, and I do not think that would be fair to Katori or Ye.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Exact priority and milestone order between the RIKEN, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups on 1e-16 and 1e-18 uncertainty; I am relying partly on memory.
Whether the redefinition of the second and the new-physics searches will be seen as realised impact or still prospective.
If the committee would rather prefer a cold-atom prize, which three of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller should be named.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B009 from my profile. My Lund background overlaps with Svanberg, Alden and the Lund Laser Centre community, but none of the credited people is a collaborator, and I spent a year of my PhD in John Hall's lab in Boulder, which is a loose link to the JILA environment of Jun Ye that I flag for the record but do not consider disqualifying. For B008 I note that I am in the WACQT management team, which is Chalmers-led and centred on superconducting qubits and overlaps institutionally with Goran Johansson, so I would not be the right person to push that candidate.
